title: Excessive disclosure by homeowner during registration/enrollment
description: During account registration and device enrollment, the homeowner may be prompted to provide more personal data than is necessary for creating the account or pairing cameras/sensors (e.g., unnecessary profile details, precise household composition, or unrelated contact data). The act of sharing this data from the source creates a disclosure risk.
assumptions: Assumes the registration/enrollment workflow requests personal attributes beyond what is strictly necessary for account creation and device onboarding.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on generic disclosure-at-source semantics; exact LINDDUN Pro subnode may differ.

title: Linkability via enrollment-flow metadata
description: Metadata on the registration/enrollment flow can enable linking of the homeowner to a specific home hub and enrolled cameras/sensors. Even if payload contents are protected, identifiers such as account ID, hub serial number, device IDs, network addresses, timestamps, or repeated enrollment patterns may allow correlation across sessions or systems.
assumptions: Assumes the flow carries stable identifiers for the account, hub, or devices, or exposes observable metadata in transit/logging.
uncertainty_note: Exact subnode is approximate; applicability depends on whether stable identifiers or observable metadata are present on this flow.

title: Identifiability through registration and device identifiers in transit
description: The data flow may directly identify the homeowner or household through personal registration data and indirectly identify them through hub serial numbers, camera/sensor identifiers, IP address, or location-related setup information. These identifiers can make the individual or household identifiable from the flow itself.
assumptions: Assumes the enrollment message includes personal account details and/or unique device or network identifiers.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; exact LINDDUN Pro node may vary by whether identification is direct or indirect.

title: Over-collection and retention of registration/enrollment data by Home Hub
description: On receipt of registration and enrollment data, the Home Hub may store or further process more personal data than necessary for operating the system, such as retaining raw onboarding details, device metadata, or household information indefinitely. The privacy threat arises at the destination because the recipient's processing and storage create unnecessary disclosure.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub persists onboarding/account/device metadata locally or forwards it onward without strict minimization and retention controls.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is best-effort; this is a destination-side disclosure/minimization issue.

title: Unawareness of how registration and enrollment data will be used
description: The homeowner may not be adequately informed by the Home Hub about what personal data is collected during account registration and device enrollment, for what purposes it will be used, how long it will be retained, and whether it will be shared with backend services or third parties. The threat arises at the destination because the recipient controls notice and transparency.
assumptions: Assumes the onboarding UX or privacy notice is incomplete, unclear, or not presented at the point of collection.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; exact LINDDUN Pro unawareness subnode may differ.

title: Non-compliant collection of account and device-enrollment data
description: The Home Hub may process registration and device-enrollment data without a valid legal basis, without obtaining required consent where needed, without honoring data-minimization requirements, or without enabling data-subject rights. This creates a compliance risk at the destination where the data is collected and processed.
assumptions: Assumes applicable privacy regulation governs the household/account/device data and that the hub vendor determines purposes/means of processing.
uncertainty_note: Exact compliance obligations depend on jurisdiction and deployment model; tree-node id is best-effort.

title: Observation of unlock-code entry reveals guest participation
description: An observer who can see or infer the communication on this flow can detect that a guest is currently attempting to access the home, even without learning the code itself. The mere existence/timing of the code-entry interaction can reveal the guest's presence or participation.
assumptions: The code entry or its signaling is observable through network traffic, wireless emissions, visible keypad interaction, or other side effects.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort because the retrieved context gives threat-type applicability but not the detailed Detecting subtree for this exact case.

title: Home Hub can identify the guest via the temporary access code
description: When the Home Hub receives the temporary access code, it may be able to map that code to a specific invited guest or invitation instance, thereby identifying the individual behind this access attempt.
assumptions: Temporary codes are unique per guest, booking, or invitation and the hub or connected backend maintains that mapping.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort subtree selection; exact I-node may vary depending on the project's threat-tree granularity.

title: Home Hub can link multiple access attempts to the same guest or invitation
description: If the same temporary code is reused across attempts or retained in logs, the Home Hub can link separate unlock attempts and related events to the same guest, building a behavioral record over time.
assumptions: The temporary code persists long enough to be reused or logged, and events are stored or correlated by code or invitation identifier.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort subtree selection; exact L-node may differ in a fuller threat-tree reference.

title: Guest may be unable to deny having attempted entry
description: If the Home Hub logs the submitted temporary code together with timestamps and outcome, those records can later be used as evidence that the guest attempted to unlock the door, reducing plausible deniability.
assumptions: The hub stores audit or event logs that associate the temporary code with a guest or invitation.
uncertainty_note: Applies only if such logs are retained and attributable.

title: Guest may be unaware that code entry is logged or correlated
description: The guest may not understand that entering a temporary access code at the Home Hub can trigger logging, correlation with an invitation, retention of timestamps, or onward sharing with other components, undermining informed expectations about processing.
assumptions: The system provides limited notice about logging, retention, or downstream use of access events.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort subtree selection; exact U-node may vary.

title: Code-entry processing may exceed the guest's expected purpose
description: The Home Hub may process the temporary access code not only to decide whether to unlock the door, but also for secondary purposes such as analytics, occupancy inference, profiling of visits, or long-term retention, which may be incompatible with the original access purpose.
assumptions: The hub or connected services retain or repurpose access-event data beyond immediate authentication and door control.
uncertainty_note: Depends on actual downstream processing and stated purposes.

title: Sensor-event logging reveals occupants' behavior patterns
description: By writing motion, door, and other sensor events to the log, the Home Hub creates a detailed record of in-home activities. Even before any later analysis, the act of recording these events can disclose presence, movement, routines, arrivals/departures, and sleep/absence patterns about household members.
assumptions: The logged events are granular enough (timestamps, event types, device identifiers) to reflect human behavior in the home.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement for disclosure via recording/storage; exact sub-node may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Local event log enables linking of multiple events to the same household or person
description: The Local Event Log aggregates repeated motion, door, and sensor events over time. This allows separate observations to be linked together into a coherent activity history for the same home, device set, or inferred individual, increasing the ability to correlate behavior across time.
assumptions: The datastore retains identifiers, timestamps, or contextual fields that let events be correlated.
uncertainty_note: Exact linkage target may be household, device, or inferred individual depending on schema.

title: Stored event history may identify residents through distinctive routines
description: Although individual sensor events may seem low sensitivity, the accumulated local log can make residents identifiable through unique temporal patterns, occupancy schedules, and combinations of device activations. This can single out a specific resident or household.
assumptions: An attacker or authorized reader can access enough historical entries to infer distinctive patterns.
uncertainty_note: Identification may be indirect and depends on access to the log plus auxiliary knowledge.

title: Local storage of raw sensor events exposes intimate household information
description: Once received by the Local Event Log, the destination stores sensitive raw event data that can reveal occupancy, habits, security-related behavior, and potentially special situations such as vacations or nighttime movement. The privacy threat arises from retaining this information in the datastore.
assumptions: The datastore preserves event timestamps and event semantics rather than only coarse aggregates.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate if a more specific disclosure-from-storage node exists in the applied catalog.

title: Residents may be unaware of the extent of local event logging
description: If the Home Hub writes all motion, door, and sensor events to the Local Event Log without clear notice or understandable controls, data subjects may not understand that detailed in-home activity histories are being retained locally.
assumptions: Users/residents are not fully informed through setup UX, policy, or device indicators about this logging behavior.
uncertainty_note: This depends strongly on product UX and transparency measures, which are not described.

title: Event logging may exceed necessity or user expectations
description: Persistently storing detailed motion, door, and sensor events in the Local Event Log may be unnecessary for the stated purpose if only short-term automation or aggregated status is needed. Retaining fine-grained raw events can therefore conflict with data minimization, storage limitation, or purpose-limitation expectations.
assumptions: The system could function with less granular logging, shorter retention, or aggregation, and no explicit necessity for full raw-event retention is established.
uncertainty_note: Necessity/compliance depends on system purpose, retention policy, and applicable requirements, which are not provided.

title: Excessive disclosure of recorded clips by the Home Hub
description: The Home Hub may upload full recorded camera clips to cloud storage even when only a subset is necessary, disclosing occupants, visitors, interiors, timestamps, and incidental bystanders beyond what is needed for the service purpose.
assumptions: Recorded clips can contain rich personal data about household members and visitors; upload scope may exceed strict necessity.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort because the retrieved context did not include detailed threat-tree node definitions.

title: Linkability via upload metadata on the clip transfer
description: Metadata on the upload flow, such as device identifiers, account identifiers, IP address, timing, clip frequency, and camera identifiers, can allow linking multiple uploads to the same household or user over time.
assumptions: Transport or application-layer metadata is observable or retained by intermediaries or the receiving service.
uncertainty_note: Specific node id is approximate due to missing detailed tree-node mapping in the provided context.

title: Identifiability from clip content and transfer metadata

assumptions: Clip content or metadata is accessible to the cloud service and may be sufficient to identify natural persons or a specific home.

title: Over-collection or over-retention of camera clips in cloud storage
description: Cloud video storage may store uploaded clips longer than necessary or retain more detail than needed for the stated purpose, increasing privacy exposure for residents and visitors.
assumptions: The cloud service defines retention and storage practices and may keep originals, backups, thumbnails, or derived data.

title: Insufficient transparency about cloud storage and downstream use
description: Individuals captured in the clips may be unaware that recordings are uploaded to cloud storage, how long they are kept, who can access them, and whether they are used for analytics, sharing, or law-enforcement requests.

uncertainty_note: Specific node id is approximate due to lack of detailed node references in the retrieved context.

title: Processing of uploaded clips without valid consent or other lawful basis
description: Cloud storage and related processing of home camera footage may occur without valid consent from all recorded individuals, or without another appropriate legal basis, especially for visitors or passersby captured incidentally.
assumptions: The system operates in a jurisdiction requiring consent or another lawful basis for recording and cloud processing of personal data.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on jurisdiction and deployment context; tree node id is approximate.

title: Lack of provable accountability for clip upload and storage actions
description: If the cloud storage service does not maintain trustworthy records of when clips were uploaded, accessed, modified, shared, or deleted, parties may be unable to prove what happened to personal footage, undermining accountability and data-subject rights handling.
assumptions: Audit logging, integrity protection, or evidentiary records may be incomplete or not exposed to relevant parties.
uncertainty_note: Non-repudiation in privacy context can be nuanced; included here as accountability for personal-data handling rather than classic security non-repudiation. Tree node id approximate.

title: Excessive disclosure of motion-alert data by the Home Hub
description: The Home Hub may forward more personal data than is strictly necessary for a real-time motion alert, such as precise timestamps, device identifiers, household identifiers, sensor metadata, or repeated event details. Because motion events can reveal occupancy and behavior patterns, unnecessary fields in the alert increase avoidable disclosure to the backend.
assumptions: Assumes the alert payload may contain metadata beyond the minimum needed to notify the backend of a motion event.

title: Linkability via recurring motion-alert transmissions
description: Repeated motion alerts sent from the same Home Hub to the backend can be linked together through stable identifiers, routing metadata, timing patterns, or persistent connection characteristics. This can enable construction of a behavioral profile for a household or device over time.

Such downstream use may be incompatible with the user's expectations for a real-time safety alert.

If the notification includes details such as time, camera/location, or thumbnail text, it can disclose presence patterns or behavior to anyone who can view the notification on the device or lock screen.
assumptions: Assumes the push notification contains event details beyond a generic app prompt, or is shown on the phone lock screen where others may see it.

description: Even if notification payload is minimized, metadata on the flow such as recipient endpoint, device token, timing, and repeated motion-event alerts can allow observers or intermediaries in the notification delivery chain to link the homeowner to a particular monitored home, device, or routine.

title: Notification displayed on the phone may disclose sensitive home-security events to bystanders
description: When the homeowner's device receives and displays the motion-detected notification, people near the device may learn that motion occurred at the home, infer occupancy status, or discover that the person uses a home-security system.
assumptions: Assumes notifications may appear on the lock screen, wearable, or other visible surfaces without redaction.
uncertainty_note: This is a destination-side disclosure threat caused by how the recipient device presents the received data; tree-node citation is approximate.

title: The homeowner may be unaware of how much information is exposed through notifications

assumptions: Assumes limited transparency or configuration guidance around notification privacy settings.
uncertainty_note: Unawareness is plausible here, but depends on product UX and notice design.

title: Notification processing may occur without sufficiently specific consent or controllable preferences
description: If motion-detected push alerts are enabled by default, or if users cannot granularly control notification content and lock-screen exposure, the homeowner may receive privacy-impacting disclosures without meaningful consent or choice.
assumptions: Assumes notification preferences are coarse-grained, default-on, or not clearly consented to.
uncertainty_note: Consent/non-compliance depends on the actual consent and settings model; included as a plausible threat rather than a certainty.

description: Even if described as aggregated device-usage analytics, the backend's disclosure to the analytics vendor can still enable linking records belonging to the same user, household, app account, or device over time if stable identifiers, quasi-identifiers, cohort keys, or fine-grained segmentation are included in the shared dataset.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics are not fully anonymized and may contain stable or repeated attributes, cohort identifiers, or dimensions that permit correlation.

title: Data in transit may reveal identifiable information through payload or metadata
description: The transfer itself can expose identifying information if the analytics payload, endpoint parameters, headers, or transport metadata contain device identifiers, account references, IP-address-derived context, or other attributes that single out users or devices.
assumptions: Assumes network-level metadata or transmitted fields are observable to parties on the path or logged by intermediaries.

title: Analytics vendor may infer sensitive behavior or attributes from aggregated usage analytics
description: Upon receipt, the cloud analytics vendor may derive information about user behavior patterns, interests, routines, or potentially sensitive categories from the shared usage analytics, especially when combined with its existing datasets or models.
assumptions: Assumes the vendor has analytical capability and the shared aggregates retain enough granularity to support inference.

title: Vendor processing may disclose information beyond the original sharing context
description: The analytics vendor may further disclose, repurpose, or make accessible the received analytics to sub-processors, affiliates, internal teams, or other customers in ways not expected by data subjects, causing information disclosure beyond the intended purpose.
assumptions: Assumes onward sharing, broad internal access, or secondary use is possible under the vendor's operating model or contract.

title: Sharing analytics with a third-party vendor may be unexpected to users
description: Users may not reasonably expect that their device-usage analytics, even in aggregated form, are sent from the backend to an external analytics vendor, particularly if this sharing is not clearly communicated or is broader than necessary for the app's core service.
assumptions: Assumes user expectations are shaped by the app's primary function and that third-party analytics sharing is not obvious from the interaction itself.
uncertainty_note: Expectation mismatch depends on transparency and product context.

title: Backend-to-vendor analytics sharing may lack valid consent or another appropriate legal basis

assumptions: Assumes the analytics data are personal data or can become personal data when combined with other information, and that applicable law requires consent or another legal basis for this third-party analytics sharing.
